item.title: LOCAL GETAWAYS | Ride and Slide | From the roof of the vessel into the crystal-clear ocean
item.description: THERE is a distinct moment, just as you clear the bustling docks of Port Denarau, where the turquoise hue of the Pacific Ocean deepens and the hum of everyday life fades entirely into the background. You are on board a sleek, high-speed catamaran, slicing through the warm tropical breeze toward Fiji’s world-famous Mamanuca Islands.
item.content:encoded:
THERE is a distinct moment, just as you clear the bustling docks of Port Denarau, where the turquoise hue of the Pacific Ocean deepens and the hum of everyday life fades entirely into the background.

You are on board a sleek, high-speed catamaran, slicing through the warm tropical breeze toward Fiji’s world-famous Mamanuca Islands.

But this is no ordinary sightseeing cruise. This is South Sea Cruises’ “Ride and Slide” excursion — a 4.5-hour half-day adventure that seamlessly blends adrenaline, luxury, and the legendary warmth of Fijian hospitality.

For travellers looking to inject a healthy dose of pure, unadulterated joy into their holiday itinerary, the ultimate highlight awaits at anchor: a giant inflatable slide plunging straight from the roof of the vessel into the crystal-clear ocean.

“Such a fun experience! I highly recommend to all,” shared Michele, a traveler from the United States, reflecting on the universal appeal of the trip.

“There were a range of young families, young adults to 50-year-olds. I think it’s safe to say every person had a blast.”

Whether you choose to launch yourself down the massive slide into the tropical waters or opt for the easy-access steps, the underwater world does not disappoint.

The catamaran anchors near vibrant coral reefs teeming with exotic marine life.

Equipped with the provided snorkeling gear, guests find themselves floating over brilliant coral gardens alongside schools of neon fish.

Even when local tropical weather misbehaves, the adventure doesn’t skip a beat.

Catherine from New Zealand noted that while the weather didn’t completely play along on her day out, her group still loved the snorkeling and the slide, as the ocean waters remained blissfully warm.

For those who want to explore the surface at a gentler pace, stand-up paddleboards are readily available. Others choose to simply swim or enjoy a sun-soaked stopover at the pristine, private island of South Sea Cay, a postcard-perfect slice of white sand surrounded by a brilliant reef.

An afternoon of aquatic exploration works up quite an appetite. Fortunately, the “Ride and Slide” experience ensures nobody goes hungry or thirsty. While on board, guests are treated to a delicious, gourmet light lunch accompanied by snacks and an endless stream of complimentary beverages. Whether your preference is a chilled local beer, a crisp house wine, or refreshing bottled water and soft drinks, the drinks flow freely alongside the laid-back tunes playing over the sound system.

“The trip was so amazing,” says Jacinta from Australia.

“The staff, the boat, the facilities were superb. A lovely lunch and good vibes.”

What truly transforms this excursion from a great day out into an unforgettable highlight of a Fijian vacation is the crew.

A team of exceptional locals keeps the energy high and the atmosphere welcoming.

Guests consistently praise their happy, personable, and encouraging nature, which coaxes even the most hesitant swimmers to try something new.

The crew’s dedication to their guests is legendary.

During one recent trip, an American visitor accidentally lost her sunglasses to the deep blue.

Without hesitation, a young crew member dove all the way down to the seabed to rescue them.

“It was truly an above and beyond act!” she recalled.

The 4.5-hour “Ride and Slide” tour departs from Port Denarau and includes pre-booked return coach transfers from most Denarau, Wailoaloa, and Nadi hotels.

The tour is perfect for swimmers aged five and up. Remember to pack your swimwear, a towel, a hat, and reef-safe sunscreen.

A guest tries out the South Sea Cruises Ride and Slide Picture South Sea Cats. INSET: South Sea Cruises new Ride and Slide attraction at the famous Mamanuca waters. Pictures: South Sea Cats

item.title: POINT OF ORIGIN I Four decades of changing lives
item.description: WHEN Veronica Angeline Narayan first arrived at the Fiji Society for the Blind (FSB) in 1985, she was a young girl from Somosomo, Naqara, Taveuni, unsure of what the future held. item.content:encoded:
WHEN Veronica Angeline Narayan first arrived at the Fiji Society for the Blind (FSB) in 1985, she was a young girl from Somosomo, Naqara, Taveuni, unsure of what the future held.

Today, four decades later, she is helping shape the futures of other visually impaired students as a braillist, producing Braille textbooks and examination papers while pursuing a Diploma in Special Education at Fiji National University.

Her story is one of many that reflects the transformation the Fiji Society for the Blind has achieved over the past 56 years.

Executive director Barbara Farouk said the organisation’s greatest achievement had been helping blind and partially sighted students move beyond special education and into mainstream schools, universities and the workforce.

“As a result, our former students were able to continue their education into high schools under our integration program, which opened doors for them to pursue tertiary education at various universities in Fiji,” she said.

“In the last 10 years some 12 of our former students were able to complete their degree program and most of them are now in permanent employments.

“At the moment we have about 15 students pursuing further education at different universities in Fiji.”

For Ms Farouk, these milestones are proof that a vision established more than half a century ago is becoming reality.

“Our organisation’s vision and mission which were set 56 years ago are now in sight.

“We are now competing and moving alongside the sighted world.”

The journey, however, has not been without obstacles.

“Obviously we’ve had challenges as we all do in life but some of our biggest challenges have been funding and finding employment for our graduates and those who drop out of school.

“Our aim is to help them lead independent and productive lives.”

Ms Farouk said the organisation’s work extended far beyond its Vatuwaqa campus.

“We have a Community Based Outreach Program with a field officer in each region to identify, train, rehabilitate and help infants, children and their families on a regular basis.”

She said the outreach program was becoming increasingly important as more younger adults lost their sight because of preventable health conditions.

“Due to uncontrolled diabetes by individuals, there are heaps of new blind and partially sighted people in their 30s.”

The community-based rehabilitation program was once funded by the Australian Government but is now entirely self-funded.

“We welcome any new donor as we provide full acquittals, are transparent and all the books are audited and up to date.”

Ms Farouk acknowledged the long list of organisations that have sustained the society over the years, including the QBE Foundation, Vodafone Fiji, Autocare, Rotary Club of Suva, Vinod Patel Foundation, Fiji Water Foundation and Brijlal.

She also thanked the people and governments of Great Britain, New Zealand, Australia, Canada, Japan and Germany for their assistance, noting that Japan donated the society’s 38-seater bus about a decade ago to transport students.

“All governments have helped FSB these past 50 years.

“Big vinaka vakalevu to all our past and current donors. There’s no way we would be here without their support.”

For Veronica Narayan, that support changed the course of her life.

“I was brought up by my grandparents,” she recalled.

“When I was identified by the Society for the Blind in 1985, I came here to learn Braille and was integrated to Saint Marcellin Primary School for my primary education, and attended Cathedral Secondary School, now known as Sacred Heart College.”

After secondary school, she returned to FSB for pre-vocational studies, learning computer skills alongside cooking, sewing, baking and other daily living skills.

An opportunity to undertake leadership training in Japan further broadened her horizons.

“I mentioned that I wanted to learn massage,” she said.

She spent 10 months in Japan, learning the language before completing practical training at a residential care facility.

item.title: EXPERIENCE I The biggest Sport in the World
item.description: Oilei! My team, the Three Lions, lost. There’s a term in iTaukei for people who can’t make up their minds, tamata veilecayaki. That pretty much summed me up. I started with team Germany. They crashed out in Round of 32, so I switched to France. Then England, the Three Lions, won me over when they held their ground against Mexico at the iconic Estadio Azteca in Mexico City – Round 16.
item.content:encoded:
Oilei! My team, the Three Lions, lost. There’s a term in iTaukei for people who can’t make up their minds, tamata veilecayaki. That pretty much summed me up.

I started with team Germany. They crashed out in Round of 32, so I switched to France. Then England, the Three Lions, won me over when they held their ground against Mexico at the iconic Estadio Azteca in Mexico City – Round 16.

From the sidelines, the coaches’ screams were drowned out by the roar of 87,500 home fans. There was so much talk even before game-time. Passionate crowds of Mexican supporters gathered outside the England team’s JW Marriott hotel in the early hours of the morning.

Armed with loudspeakers, horns, and fireworks, they attempted to disrupt the players’ sleep in a traditional Latin American “serenade”. But that wasn’t enough for Jude Bellingham and Harry Kane.

The Three Lions made the semi-finals but were swept off their feet by a more classy and spirited Spain side. It was the Spain’s prodigy Lamine Yamal who caught my attention more than Messi. The 19-year-old playing with so much rhythm, and so I joined the Spanish bandwagon.

Hey! There is no Tier 1 or Tier 2 category in World Cup soccer. Anybody could win. These were pro players sitting on multi-million-dollar salaries, so I prefer to keep my options open.

This year’s FIFA World Cup lasted 39 days, running from June 11 to July 19, 2026.

The World Cup hype was introduced to me by my dad, an avid soccer fan from his days in old Flagstaff, Suva, in the early ’90s, just after Fiji began broadcasting free-to-air television nationwide for the very first time.

Our TV screen brought neighbours and friends to our home. My dad’s team was Germany. His friends had their own teams. They were drinking grog in the living room, watching the games, when I walked in to use the video deck to watch a movie.

“Sit down, boy, and watch the World Cup. You might learn something here,” dad said.

The living room was lively. Even my mum was there as well. Back then, I wouldn’t dare speak back to my parents. So I sat down to watch. There was so much commotion that evening. And boy, did that moment change my perspective about World Cup soccer. This was soccer of a different category.

Not the “kick the ball in front and everybody chases” technique. We see a lot of that locally. This was ball control, accurate passes, and skill. Whenever his team would gain possession of the ball, my dad’s favourite cheer was, “Taki! Taki!… taki!”, meaning to serve the grog immediately. And in 1994, Germany had a good team. Despite the protests against the fast taki, while watching the games, dad would respond, “Gunu yani!” (drink up).

Unbelievable stories of past World Cup events

“Maaaraaadooona!” was the name I heard spoken with such amusement.

“Hia hiah, the Hand of God,” one of dad’s friends said.

He said soccer fans all over the world know the story.

“Maradona was the guy who could dribble through the defence just to score, but only one thing… the fella took too much drugs.”

In the ’80s, Argentina football legend Diego Maradona was a superstar like the great Pelé of Brazil. A number of parents named their children after Diego Maradona following his historic performance in the 1986 World Cup.

A wizard with the ball, he scored against England in the quarter-final with his hand, and the referee missed it, allowing Argentina to win 2-1 over England in 1986. There was no VAR then, and this became one of the biggest controversies in soccer history.

His last World Cup was in 1994, where he played two games before being sent home and suspended for failing a drug test for ephedrine. Maradona struggled with drug addiction, primarily cocaine, which severely impacted his career and personal life.

Another player known as “Italy’s saviour” for the four-time world champions was Roberto Baggio. A midfielder loaded with passion and skill, he almost carried Italy through the 1994 USA tournament.

Italy wouldn’t have made it without their maestro, Baggio, but what happened in the final turned their hero into a villain. Later, a movie was made depicting Baggio’s fast descent into depression, all because he missed a crucial penalty.

On July 17, Roberto Baggio, knowing that failure to score would consign Italy to defeat and confirm Brazil as champions, struck the ball well above the crossbar, sending his own team home.

Baggio experienced a deeply divided aftermath in Italy, transitioning from widespread sympathy and lingering reverence among true fans to extreme vitriol from harsh critics. The immediate reaction from some angry fans was severe, with graffiti famously appearing on walls declaring, “God will forgive everyone except Baggio.”

Also in 1994, Diana Ross’s opening ceremony performance featured a choreographed scene where she was to kick a goal to signify the opening of the FIFA World Cup. The legendary singer ran onto the field in a red pyjama suit while lip-syncing “I’m Coming Out”.

She jogged all the way to the penalty box and, instead of easily tapping the ball past the goalkeeper (who had notably stepped well off his line), she sliced the shot completely wide. The scene became the talk of the world. Some called it “Diana Ross’s awful penalty miss”.

This 2026 tournament also had its own controversies.

The first involved US striker Folarin Balogun receiving a red card against Bosnia and Herzegovina, which carried an automatic one-match suspension. Following a direct phone call from US President Donald Trump to FIFA President Gianni Infantino, FIFA’s disciplinary committee suspended the ban.

Then Iran’s disallowed goal in their final group-stage match against Egypt. Iran had a stoppage-time goal ruled out by VAR for a millimetre offside. That decision denied Iran a place in the knockout stage. The coach and players lashed out at FIFA during a press conference.

On the field, the coach was shown a yellow card for his defiance after raising his arms to gesture a cross in the faces of officials, claiming they had stolen the game from Iran.

item.title: UNITY I Reconciliation and a shared future
item.description: FIJI is one of the Pacific’s most culturally diverse nations. Indigenous iTaukei, Indo-Fijians, Rotumans, Pacific Islanders, Europeans, Chinese and many other communities have shaped the country’s development while maintaining distinct cultural and religious identities. This diversity is one of Fiji’s greatest strengths, but diversity alone does not create social cohesion. It must be supported by
item.content:encoded:
FIJI is one of the Pacific’s most culturally diverse nations. Indigenous iTaukei, Indo-Fijians, Rotumans, Pacific Islanders, Europeans, Chinese and many other communities have shaped the country’s development while maintaining distinct cultural and religious identities. This diversity is one of Fiji’s greatest strengths, but diversity alone does not create social cohesion. It must be supported by institutions, shared values and everyday practices that encourage mutual respect, equal participation and a common sense of belonging.

Multiculturalism should therefore extend beyond festivals, ceremonies and symbolic celebrations. While shared meals and cultural events encourage interaction, reconciliation requires something deeper: understanding one another’s histories, recognising the contributions of every community and accepting that Fiji’s future depends on all its citizens. A society that merely tolerates diversity remains vulnerable to misunderstanding, whereas one that embraces diversity as a source of collective strength becomes more resilient.

The familiar expressions of the Bula spirit and Salaam represent more than hospitality. They reflect values of goodwill, respect and peaceful coexistence that should shape everyday life—in schools, workplaces, neighbourhoods and public institutions. Reconciliation is measured not by slogans but by the quality of relationships between ordinary citizens.

This raises important questions. Do all communities experience an equal sense of belonging? Does national identity embrace every citizen regardless of ethnicity or religion? Are opportunities shared fairly, and are diverse voices genuinely heard? These questions lie at the heart of democratic nation-building and deserve continuing reflection.

Building an inclusive society begins with understanding. People should know and value the traditions, history and beliefs of their own communities. Confidence in one’s identity reduces the insecurity that often fuels prejudice.

At the same time, reconciliation requires openness to learning about others. Respectful engagement across cultures broadens understanding, challenges stereotypes and reveals shared aspirations while acknowledging genuine differences in language, belief and custom. In an increasingly interconnected world, this capacity is essential both within Fiji and in its engagement with the wider Pacific and global community.

Meaningful multiculturalism depends on cultural self-awareness, effective communication across differences, appreciation of the histories of all communities and the ability to consider issues from multiple perspectives. It also requires recognising the contributions each community has made to national development while respecting traditions different from one’s own.

Reconciliation ultimately depends upon the values that guide public life. Political institutions alone cannot sustain democracy if citizens lose confidence in one another or if sections of society feel excluded. Social cohesion grows when people believe they are treated fairly, respected equally and able to contribute to the common good.

Respect affirms the equal dignity of every person regardless of race, religion, gender or social background. It rejects discrimination and recognises diversity as a permanent feature of Fiji’s national identity.

Compassion encourages empathy rather than suspicion. Historical suffering should deepen understanding instead of becoming a justification for future division.

Trust develops gradually through honesty, fairness and consistent leadership. It cannot be legislated but must be earned through the conduct of individuals, institutions and public leaders.

Justice requires laws to apply equally to every citizen and public institutions to remain impartial in protecting rights and resolving disputes. Confidence in democracy depends on the belief that institutions serve all communities fairly.

Shared prosperity recognises that economic opportunity and national development should benefit every section of society. Inclusive growth strengthens social stability by reinforcing the belief that every citizen has a stake in Fiji’s future.

The work of reconciliation now takes place in a communication environment transformed by digital technology. Social media has expanded access to information and public debate but has also accelerated the spread of misinformation, prejudice and extremist narratives.

Religious communities therefore carry an important responsibility. Sound teaching must remain accessible, relevant and responsive to contemporary challenges. Faith leaders are no longer confined to places of worship; they must also engage responsibly through digital platforms where many young people seek guidance.

This responsibility extends to every faith community. Freedom of religion is a cornerstone of democratic society, but it carries a corresponding obligation to reject hatred, exclusion and intolerance while promoting peace, respect and responsible citizenship.

Young people deserve particular attention. They do not automatically inherit either the divisions or the wisdom of previous generations. Their understanding of diversity, democracy and national identity will largely determine the strength of Fiji’s future social cohesion.

A Muslim identity within a democratic Fiji

For Fiji’s Muslims, religious identity has never been separate from civic responsibility. Islam encourages participation in society rather than withdrawal from it. A faithful Muslim is expected to contribute positively to family, community and nation while remaining true to religious principles.

This understanding has enabled Muslims to maintain their religious identity while participating confidently in a secular democratic state. Islamic values emphasise honesty, justice, compassion, education, service and respect for lawful authority—principles that reinforce democratic citizenship rather than undermine it.

Accordingly, the Muslim community continues to preserve its religious traditions while adapting constructively to changing social realities. It values education, intellectual inquiry and an understanding of both Islamic civilisation and the wider world. It respects other faiths while remaining confident in its own beliefs and seeks to be recognised not merely as a religious minority but as an active partner in Fiji’s national development.

Pluralism does not require communities to abandon deeply held convictions. It requires respect for the equal rights of others and a willingness to work together for the common good.

The experience of the past four decades offers important lessons. Political stability, while essential, is not enough if trust remains fragile. Lasting reconciliation requires sustained investment in the institutions and relationships that unite people.

Education will continue to play a central role. Schools should prepare students not only for employment but also for democratic citizenship by fostering critical thinking, ethical responsibility and appreciation of Fiji’s diverse heritage. Every young person should understand the histories, traditions and contributions of the communities that call Fiji home.

Families are equally important because they are where children first learn respect, empathy and responsibility. Parents and grandparents therefore shape future citizens long before schools and public institutions do.

Religious organisations should continue promoting ethical leadership, social responsibility and peaceful coexistence. Their influence extends beyond worship into the moral life of society.Community organisations also have an important role by creating opportunities for people of different backgrounds to work together through education, sport, environmental initiatives, disaster response and voluntary service. Shared experience often builds stronger relationships than dialogue alone.

Public institutions must continue demonstrating fairness, transparency and accountability. Equal treatment before the law strengthens confidence in democracy and reassures citizens that their rights are protected regardless of identity.

Ultimately, reconciliation depends on the participation of every citizen.

The experience of Fiji’s Muslim community reflects a broader national story. Like many other communities, Muslims experienced the uncertainty, displacement and loss associated with political upheaval. They witnessed migration, weakened institutions and diminished public trust. Yet they also demonstrated resilience by rebuilding community organisations, investing in education, strengthening families and continuing to serve the wider society.

These experiences offer lessons that extend beyond one religious community. Reconciliation is achieved not by forgetting the past but by learning from it. A peaceful society is sustained through justice, education, dialogue, responsible leadership and recognition of the equal dignity of every citizen.

item.title: CAREER I Fiji’s creative future
item.description: THE rapid growth of Fiji’s creative industry has brought with it a new generation of photographers, filmmakers, graphic designers and digital storytellers eager to make their mark. Social media has lowered barriers to entry, affordable technology has placed professional-grade equipment within reach, and artificial intelligence has begun reshaping the way creative work is produced.
item.content:encoded:
THE rapid growth of Fiji’s creative industry has brought with it a new generation of photographers, filmmakers, graphic designers and digital storytellers eager to make their mark.

Social media has lowered barriers to entry, affordable technology has placed professional-grade equipment within reach, and artificial intelligence has begun reshaping the way creative work is produced.

Yet beneath this expanding landscape lies an industry still searching for structure.

According to Ben Seniroqa, founder of Only Idea Studios, Fiji’s creative sector is rich with talent but held back by gaps in business knowledge, limited investment and an education system that has yet to fully embrace creative careers.

Nonetheless, he believes the prospects are promising for visual and creative arts space.

“I think the industry is in a good place,” he said.

“There are many talented young content creators producing excellent work.”

Having spent years working behind the scenes for production companies before taking Only Idea Studios directly to clients, Ben has watched Fiji’s creative economy evolve from an emerging niche into an increasingly competitive marketplace.

One of his biggest concerns is the absence of common business standards, particularly around pricing.

In today’s market, he said, two creatives can quote vastly different prices for work of a similar nature.

While experienced professionals price projects based on years of knowledge, equipment costs and production requirements, newcomers often undercharge as they build portfolios.

The result is an uneven market where clients struggle to understand the true value of creative work.

“You might have one videographer charging $3000 for a project while another charges only $200 for something very similar,” he said.

Without greater understanding of how projects are costed, he believes unrealistic expectations become embedded across the industry.

Rather than calling for regulation, Ben believes mentorship and greater openness among experienced practitioners would help emerging creatives understand not only their craft but also how to operate sustainable businesses.

The challenge, however, extends beyond pricing.

Running a creative business requires far more than artistic ability.

It involves managing clients, complying with tax obligations, paying staff, investing in equipment and maintaining professional standards.

These are lessons Ben largely learned through experience.

“My generation learned largely through trial and error,” he said.

“We had to teach ourselves, make mistakes and gradually build experience.”

That experience has shaped another conviction—that Fiji’s education system needs to evolve alongside changing industries.

While schools have traditionally focused on academic subjects and sports, Ben believes creative disciplines such as photography, videography, animation and digital design deserve far greater recognition.

Today’s students are growing up immersed in technology, he said, yet many leave school with little exposure to careers that increasingly contribute to Fiji’s economy.

He sees creative industries as more than artistic pursuits.

Journalists, musicians, filmmakers, designers and content creators all generate employment, support tourism and help shape Fiji’s cultural identity.

Preparing young people for these careers should begin in the classroom rather than after they enter the workforce.

Although home studios have enabled many creatives to produce quality work, Ben believes Fiji lacks dedicated production facilities where professionals can collaborate using industry-standard equipment.

Such infrastructure would strengthen local capacity and reduce reliance on overseas resources.

When discussing government support, however, Ben highlighted that funding alone is not the centre of the conversation.

item.title: DISCOVERING FIJI I Rev Thomas Baker (Part 1)
item.description: LONG before Reverend Thomas Baker’s name became forever linked with one of Fiji’s most tragic chapters, it was tied to something far quieter, a deep conviction that his life’s work lay among the people of the islands. His own words, written years before his death reveal not fear but anticipation, a man convinced he had found his purpose.
item.content:encoded:
LONG before Reverend Thomas Baker’s name became forever linked with one of Fiji’s most tragic chapters, it was tied to something far quieter, a deep conviction that his life’s work lay among the people of the islands.

His own words, written years before his death reveal not fear but anticipation, a man convinced he had found his purpose.

“When I knew I was to go to Fiji I felt my spirit was glad,” he wrote in his diary on February 18, 1859.

“To this place I felt my spirit irresistibly drawn, and now I have my heart’s desire.”

Those diary entries, together with accounts preserved in The Missionary Worthies by Reverend William Moister, correspondence published in Missionary Enterprise and Home Service – An Autobiography by John S. Austin, and records from FamilySearch, paint the portrait of a missionary whose brief ministry was marked by unwavering faithfulness.

The Missionary Worthies by Reverend William Moister, kept at the Camden Theological Library archives highlight that Thomas Baker was born at Playden, Sussex in England, on February 6, 1832, to Jeremiah Baker and Harriett Elizabeth Vinten.

When he was eight years old, the family migrated to Australia where his life would take a direction he could scarcely have imagined.

Drawn by his love of singing, Baker began attending a Wesleyan church in Sydney.

There, according to Reverend Moister, he came “under the Ministry of the Word,” became convinced of sin and “soon experienced acceptance with God.”

His faith quickly became evident through his service.

After joining the Wesleyan Society, his “consistent piety and ardent zeal” led to his appointment as a class leader and local preacher.

In 1859 he married Harriett Moon in Chippendale, New South Wales. That same year he was accepted as a probationer by the Australian Wesleyan Conference and appointed as a missionary to Fiji.

The appointment was exactly what he had hoped for.

“And now I have great work to perform,” Reverend Baker wrote in his journal.

“I know God is my helper and in the strength of Grace I go far hence to the Gentiles.”

He believed the Gospel could reach even the darkest places.

“Truly the dark places of the earth are full of habitants of cruelty. But their darkness can be expelled by the light of the Gospel.”

Baker travelled to Fiji with Reverend Joseph Waterhouse and other missionaries, arriving on April 25, 1859, after a 16-day voyage aboard the John Wesley.

His first impressions of the islands reflected both admiration and the challenges ahead.

“My sickness for the first three days hindered me from enjoying the passage. My wife was very sick also,” he wrote.

“The John Wesley is one of the best cradles I ever was in.”

“I see here a very large field open to my view for missionary labour. The work appears to be very rough, plenty travelling by water.”

Despite the unfamiliar surroundings, Baker immersed himself in learning the Fijian language.

Reverend Moister records that before the end of Baker’s first year he was already preaching the Gospel in Fijian.

For more than eight years he served in the Bau, Cakaudrove, Bua and Rewa Circuits, gaining experience while frequently travelling through difficult terrain and by sea.

He often expressed a desire to work where the need was greatest and was delighted when appointed to Rewa.

There he regularly visited villages beyond established Christian communities, seeking to share his faith among those who had yet to embrace Christianity.

Letters Baker sent to his friend, Methodist Minister John S. Austin, offer a rare glimpse into daily missionary life in Fiji during the 1860s.

Writing on March 30, 1866, after moving from Bua into the interior of Viti Levu, Baker described living at what he considered the frontier between Christian and non-Christian communities.

“We have removed from Bua to the interior of large Fiji, the stronghold of Heathenism and a very large and important circuit,” he wrote.

item.title: CLIMATE SCIENCE I When highlands to the coasts shivered
item.description: THE July 2026 cold spell serves as a stark reminder that Fiji’s climate is governed by massive, natural synoptic systems rather than singular climate anomalies. As WMO accredited Class 1 Professional Meteorologist, it is essential for me to frame this event through the lens of atmospheric physics: a powerful, quasi-stationary high-pressure system—which registered a provisional record-breaking mean
item.content:encoded:
THE July 2026 cold spell serves as a stark reminder that Fiji’s climate is governed by massive, natural synoptic systems rather than singular climate anomalies.

As WMO accredited Class 1 Professional Meteorologist, it is essential for me to frame this event through the lens of atmospheric physics: a powerful, quasi-stationary high-pressure system—which registered a provisional record-breaking mean sea level pressure of 1044.5 hPa near Ouse, Tasmania, on July 6, 2026—acted as a giant atmospheric pump.

This high-pressure system was intensified by a deep low-pressure system lingering over the Tasman Sea, a process known as anticyclonic intensification, where diverging air from the upper levels of the low fed into the high-pressure system, forcing air to subside and intensify at the surface.

This synoptic setup established a persistent meridional flow, effectively funnelling a deep reservoir of polar-origin air masses directly into the tropical latitudes, including Fiji.

To understand why this cold spell was so pervasive, one must look at the “weather engine” driving the entire region. The blocking high-pressure system did not merely drift across the map; it stalled. In meteorology, we refer to this as a “blocking high”—a strong system that forms further south than usual and remains nearly stationary.

This effectively “blocked” the typical west-to-east progression of weather systems across the Southern Hemisphere, locking a specific atmospheric state in place for over a week.

The intensification was fuelled by a deep low-pressure system sitting over the Tasman Sea. When a high and a low pair in this specific configuration, they create a “blocking pair,” which serves to mutually reinforce the strength of both systems. As air converged in the upper atmosphere, it subsided rapidly, creating a process of divergence at the surface that intensified the high to historic levels.

This generated a steep pressure gradient, transforming the region into a potent meridional conduit that drew a massive, coherent air mass from high latitudes and funnelled it directly into the tropical South Pacific.

Unlike transient weather fluctuations that pass in a matter of hours, this cold air mass stagnated over the region, creating a sustained “cool-down” effect that refused to dissipate, replacing the typical tropical maritime air with a polar-origin mass.

The intensity of this event was felt cohesively across the Fiji Group, revealing a national drop in temperatures that defied the typical tropical baseline. In the Western Division, covering Nadi, Lautoka, and Ba, the cold air mass pushed minimums significantly lower than typical July averages.

Even in these traditionally warmer regions, where residents are accustomed to the reliable warmth of the leeward side, the persistence of the high-pressure system ensured that nights remained unusually chilly, with breezy conditions adding to the cooling effect. Moving to the Eastern Division, including Lauthala Bay, Nausori, and Navua, the impact was even more pronounced.

The eastern coast, often directly subject to the persistent southeasterly trade winds, bore the full brunt of this advection. Navua, in particular, shattered records on July 5, 2026, dropping to 13.8°C—the lowest reading since observations began there in 2010.

This impact was mirrored in the Maritime Groups, where stations at Matei, Vanuabalavu, and Kadavu confirmed the widespread nature of the event. Matei Airfield recorded 14.5°C on July 10, the lowest since 1956, while Vanuabalavu hit 14.6°C on July 3, the lowest since 1985. These isolated stations provided the clearest evidence that this was a total regional air-mass replacement rather than a localized fluctuation.

While Nadarivatu remained the coldest point, bottoming out at 9.7°C, the Fiji Meteorological Service noted this was not a new record, but rather a validation of its status as the nation’s traditional highland “cold trap.” It should be noted that these are only sparse point observations, and many locations across Fiji who do not have observations, multiple locations would have hit extreme lows.

Nadarivatu’s role as Fiji’s “cold trap” is rooted in its unique topography, perched at an elevation of over 800 meters. Historically, this geography has allowed for temperate-zone agriculture, including potatoes and experimental apple orchards, which thrive in these cooler microclimates that remain impossible to cultivate on the coast.

The colonial-era use of Nadarivatu as a sanatorium further underscores how distinct this highland climate is from the coastal tropical norm, serving as a retreat for those seeking relief from the humidity. During this July event, the 9.7°C reading was not a statistical anomaly but a validation of its high-altitude role as the country’s natural thermometer.

For the local farmers, this cold spell was an intensification of the “cool and dry season” mechanism that defines their agricultural cycles. It highlights how elevation and topography dictate localized outcomes even when a singular air mass blankets the entire country.

The “record-breaking” nature of this event was magnified by the clear, dry conditions that accompanied the high-pressure system. With the sky devoid of cloud cover, Fiji experienced intense nocturnal radiative cooling, where heat from the surface escaped rapidly into the upper atmosphere.

In a three-dimensional sense, the atmosphere was effectively “layered,” with the dense, cold air mass trapped near the surface and unable to dissipate due to the lack of turbulent vertical mixing. This stability, combined with the daily replenishment of cold air from the Southern Ocean, meant that the “chill” was an enduring state for the entire archipelago rather than a passing front.

Because the air was dry, it lacked the moisture content to form clouds that might otherwise trap outgoing longwave radiation. Consequently, the ground cooled rapidly during the night, leading to the remarkably low minimums that residents across Fiji felt, regardless of whether they were in a coastal or inland valley.

This synoptic configuration extended its reach far beyond the Fiji Group. While Fiji basked in cool, dry stability, the deep low-pressure system driving the high brought severe weather to our neighbours.

In New Zealand, the system developed out of the Southern Ocean as a large, slow-moving low that drew cold air north, creating widespread convection and intense rainfall that overwhelmed infrastructure in places like Wellington.

This was not a tropical storm, but rather a cold-core low that produced localized downpours as it moved over the unusually warm Tasman Sea. Meanwhile, in southeastern Australia, the core of the high-pressure system caused temperatures to plunge, with areas like Coldstream dropping to -2.7°C and parts of Tasmania hitting -8.1°C, accompanied by dense fog and widespread frost.

This regional variety is the very definition of natural synoptic variability. It serves as a reminder that our weather is the product of complex interactions between air masses, pressure systems, and topography.

This event is a testament to the fascinating complexity of our regional climate system. It is a reminder that in the South Pacific, the movement of high-pressure engines can redefine the baseline of our daily weather, testing our tropical resilience and highlighting the raw, shifting physics that govern the weather we experience every day.

There is no cause for alarm; we have simply witnessed the atmospheric gears of the South Pacific shifting into a rare, high-intensity configuration, providing a brief but memorable respite from our typical tropical warmth, and high humidities leading to discomfort.

It is a classic demonstration of how large-scale, stationary high-pressure systems behave when they lock into place, reordering the climate of the entire region. We have observed the full force of a historically record breaking 1044.5 hPa high pressure, and in doing so, we have seen the natural variability of our planet at work—a humbling display of the meteorology that shapes our lives.

Dr SUSHIL K SHARMA (BA MA MEng (RMIT) PhD (Melbourne)) is a former World Meteorological Organisation (WMO) Accredited Class 1 Professional Meteorologist; Former British Aerospace, The Royal Saudi Air Force and Bahrain Air Navigation Directorate Aviation Meteorologist; Former Associate Professor of Meteorology, Fiji National University, and former Operational Meteorologist and Manager, Climate Research and Services Division, Fiji Meteorological Services. item.title: WOMEN I Charting her own course
item.description: JANET Reddy still remembers one of the people who shaped the way she sees the world. Growing up, the late Justice Jai Ram Reddy was more than a distinguished statesman, jurist and constitutional architect.
item.content:encoded:
JANET Reddy still remembers one of the people who shaped the way she sees the world.

Growing up, the late Justice Jai Ram Reddy was more than a distinguished statesman, jurist and constitutional architect.

His granddaughter, embodied the values of service, unity and thoughtful leadership.

Among the many lessons he left behind were his passion for genuine national unity and finding common ground, ideals that remain etched in Janet’s mind.

Years later, those values continue to guide the young environmental scientist as she prepares to begin a fully funded PhD in Marine Science and Conservation at Duke University in the United States, following her graduation from Cornell University, where she became the first Fijian known to complete an undergraduate degree at the Ivy League institution.

Although the pursuit for knowledge has taken her from a small farm outside Lautoka to some of the world’s leading universities, Janet said her purpose has never changed.

It is about giving back to Fiji by protecting the oceans that have shaped both the country’s identity and its future.

Janet completed her primary education at Drasa Avenue Primary School before attending Natabua High School, where she excelled in the sciences.

Leaving Fiji after Year 12 to study in the United States was both exciting and daunting.

She enrolled in Cornell University’s Environment and Sustainability programme without knowing exactly where her journey would lead.

“I wasn’t completely sure what I wanted to specialise in,” she said.

Rather than choosing a single pathway, she designed her own interdisciplinary concentration in Marine Conservation and Management.

“I’ve always been interested in bringing together science, policy and community perspectives.

“I wanted to combine my science background with studies in policy and decision-making because it’s one thing to produce scientific knowledge, but it’s equally important that decision-makers understand that science and that scientists understand the realities of policy.”

She said researchers and policymakers often speak different technical languages.

“Good decisions require everyone to work from the same understanding.”

While science has become her profession, public service has long been part of her family’s story.

She speaks warmly of her grandfather, Justice Jai Ram Reddy, whose speeches and commitment to national reconciliation continue to influence her thinking.

“Whenever I think about Fiji’s future, I often come back to that message,” she said.

“If I had to reduce Justice Jai Ram Reddy’s message to one word, it would be unity.”

For Janet, unity is not about ignoring differences but recognising that diversity strengthens a nation.

“We all have different histories, cultures and life experiences, but the important question is how those individual experiences contribute to a shared future.

“At the end of the day, we’re all Fijians.”

That philosophy was reinforced while representing Fiji and other Small Island Developing States as a United Nations Scotland Earth Ambassador.

Working alongside young leaders from around the world, she realised that diversity was not something that divided people but strengthened collective efforts towards a sustainable future.

Cornell challenged Janet academically and personally.

When she graduated earlier this year, she discovered she was believed to be the first Fiji-born student to graduate from the university.

“It filled me with immense pride, not simply as a personal achievement, but because of what it represented for Fiji and the Pacific.”

Initially searching for fellow Fijians and Pacific Islanders, she eventually realised that belonging extended beyond geography.

“My upbringing in Fiji gave me my foundation, while my experiences overseas broadened my perspective.
